title: Open chain stitch
subtitle: A ladder-like band of open loops worked between two parallel lines
excerpt: Open chain stitch, sometimes called square chain or ladder stitch, forms a flat band of rectangular loops between two parallel lines. Each loop is left open at the sides rather than linked through itself, giving a ladder effect. It works well as a filling band or as a framework to lay a contrasting colour underneath.
sourceNotes: Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886); Caulfeild & Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

glossaryTerms.definition: The drawn or traced line on the fabric that guides where the stitches go.
The length of thread currently being stitched with, running from the fabric to the needle.

content.text: Open chain stitch is worked between two parallel
transfer lines
drawn on the fabric, typically 4 to 8 mm apart. Unlike ordinary chain stitch, each loop is not pulled closed at the top but left wide, so the
working thread
spans the full width of the band at every step. The result is a series of rectangular frames rather than oval links.
What you need

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 2 to 4 strands; pearl cotton No. 8 or No. 5

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Closely woven linen or cotton; avoid loose weaves that make straight lines hard to keep

items.label: Hoop
items.value: Round or oval hoop to keep fabric taut; essential for even loop width

content.text: Working the stitch
Draw two parallel lines on the fabric, the left line and the right line. Secure the thread on the back and bring the needle up at point A on the left line, at the top of your band.

Insert the needle at point B on the right line, level with A. Bring it up again at point C, which is a short distance below B and still on the right line. Before pulling through, lay the thread under the needle tip so the loop sits across the full width of the band.
Pull the thread through gently. The loop locks at C on the right side. You now have a half-formed rectangle: the top bar runs from A to B, and the right side runs from B down to C.

Insert the needle at point D on the left line, level with C, then bring it up at point E below D on the left line. Again lay the thread under the needle tip before pulling through. This closes the bottom of the first rectangle and starts the left side of the next.
Continue alternating: right line then left line, always placing the thread under the needle. Keep the spacing between each pair of entry points equal so the rectangles stay uniform in height.
To finish, take the needle down through both sides of the last open loop to close it into a small bar, then fasten the thread on the back.
Common mistakes

items.cause: The needle is not entering exactly on the parallel lines at each step.
items.fix: Rule light pencil lines and stitch directly along them. Check each entry point before pulling the thread through.

items.symptom: Loops pull shut and look like ordinary chain stitch
items.cause: Too much tension when drawing the thread through, or the thread is not laid under the needle before pulling.
items.fix: Use less tension and always check the thread is under the needle tip before each pull-through. Work in a hoop to keep fabric from puckering.

content.text: Uses and related stitches
Open chain stitch is a natural partner to
chain stitch
, sharing the same looping principle but on a wider band.
Cable chain stitch
adds a linking bar between loops for a heavier, more textured line.
Feathered chain stitch
branches the loops alternately to make a zig-zag band.
